title: The Small Amman Factory Samih Darwazah Bet on Quality
dek: In 1978 a Palestinian-born pharmacist left a career at Eli Lilly behind, went home to Amman and started a drug maker on the promise of reliable medicines.

story.event: Leaving Eli Lilly to found a drug maker in Amman on a bet that quality would win doctors' trust
story.summary: Samih Darwazah, a Palestinian-born pharmacist who worked for Eli Lilly from 1964 to 1976, moved back to Amman and founded Hikma in 1978 from a small factory, betting that safe, reliable medicines would win the confidence of doctors despite strong regional competition. Small profits were reinvested, payment was sometimes taken in barter, and in 1996 Hikma became, by its own account, the first Arab company to receive US FDA approval; it listed in London in 2005.
paragraphs: Samih Darwazah's working life had been a series of moves. Born in Nablus in 1930, he grew up in Jaffa, where his father was a merchant, and in 1948 the family left for Jordan. He studied pharmacy at the American University of Beirut, worked as a pharmacist in Jordan and Kuwait, then went to St Louis on a Fulbright scholarship. From 1964 to 1976 he worked for Eli Lilly, moving between regional offices in the United States, Europe and the Middle East.

By the mid-1970s, according to a profile by the American University of Beirut, he wanted a permanent home for his family and a new challenge. In 1978, at 48, he moved back to Amman and founded a drug company of his own, Hikma. The university called it a considerable risk, since the region already had plenty of competition. His wager, it said, was that truly safe and reliable medicines would in time win the confidence of suppliers and doctors. The company began as a small factory, and whatever small profit it made went back in, including into research on new and better products. His four children joined in its early days.

There followed, the profile says, years of hard work and occasional setbacks. Getting paid across the region was a difficulty of its own. A case study by the American University in Cairo's business school, summarised by Wamda, says Hikma for a time took peanuts in Syria and sesame in Sudan in trade, and accepted letters of credit in Iraq that ran for two years. From 1980 it also made patented medicines under licence. In the early years Darwazah focused on winning approval from the US Food and Drug Administration and on selling into Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.

The approval came in 1996, when, by Hikma's own timeline, it became the first Arab company to receive it. By then Hikma had bought West-Ward, a generic maker in New Jersey, and begun building an injectables plant in Portugal; the university profile describes the American business as something once believed impossible. Darwazah served as Jordan's energy minister in 1995 and 1996. Hikma listed in London in 2005 and entered the FTSE 100 in March 2015, two months before he died, with 7,000 employees.

quote.text: it is the visible, the tangible, that goes a long ways in softening prejudices. The actual sight of a first-class house that a Negro has built is ten times more potent than pages of discussion about a house that he ought to build, or perhaps could build.
quote.locator: Chapter X, "A Harder Task Than Making Bricks Without Straw"
quote.source_title: Up from Slavery: An Autobiography, Project Gutenberg eBook #2376
quote.connection: Washington, writing about Tuskegee's student brickmakers, held that a well-made thing people can see does more against doubt than any argument. Darwazah's wager was of the same kind: that medicines others could inspect, and in the end an American approval, would earn a confidence that claims alone could not.

reflection: Darwazah's bet took eighteen years to be proved in the way he had aimed at. In between came barter deals, licensed products and small profits poured back into the factory: the unglamorous work of staying open while the standard was being earned.

You may be somewhere in your own long middle, where the work is good but the proof others want has not arrived. Washington's point is a quiet comfort. People are persuaded less by what you say you could build than by what they can see you have built. That kind of proof grows slowly, and it is allowed to.
invitation: Pick one claim you often make about your work and ask what someone could see or check that would show it. If there is nothing yet, write down the smallest thing that would.

sources.supports: Born in Nablus in 1930; family in Jaffa, father a merchant; left for Jordan in 1948; pharmacy degree at AUB in 1954; worked in pharmacy in Jordan and Kuwait; Fulbright to St Louis College of Pharmacy; Eli Lilly 1964 to 1976, first in the US then in the Middle East marketing division; at 48 returned to Jordan and founded Hikma in Amman in 1978; vision of high-quality, affordable medicines; grew from a small factory with the help of his children, who joined early; minister of energy from 1995; London listing in 2005; FTSE 100 in March 2015; 7,000 employees; died on 15 May 2015 in London aged 85.

cross_checks.claim: Darwazah worked for Eli Lilly from 1964 to 1976 and founded Hikma in Amman in 1978.
He founded the company as a considerable risk against regional competition, betting on safe, reliable, high-quality medicines.
Hikma began as a small factory and his children joined the business.
In 1996 Hikma became the first Arab company to receive US FDA approval.
Hikma entered the US by buying West-Ward in New Jersey in the early 1990s and built an injectables plant in Portugal.

research_notes: Founding year: Hikma, the AUB doctorate profile and Wamda give 1978; the AUB Olayan School page and a 2008 Zawya release say 1977, and Hikma's 2015 annual report says the original holding company was incorporated in 1977 (when Deloitte were appointed auditors). The story uses 1978, when manufacturing began in Amman, and notes 1977 as the incorporation year. Age: Hikma says he was 48 when he returned to found the company, which fits 1978 for a man born in 1930. Location at Lilly: Hikma says first in the US and then in the Middle East marketing division; AUB says regional offices in the US, Europe and the Middle East; Wamda says he spent 12 years in Italy. The story uses AUB's wording. West-Ward: 1991 in Hikma's 2010 timeline and Wamda, 1992 in Hikma's 2015 annual report; the story says only that it had been bought by 1996. FDA approval: Hikma's timeline says that in 1996 it became the first Arab company to receive FDA approval and its current page speaks of the region's first FDA-inspected plant; Wikipedia says that in August 1996 it became the first Arab company to export medicines to the US; Wamda links the milestone to making West-Ward FDA compliant; a Jordan Times tribute (blocked to automated readers, so not cited) reportedly quotes a colleague dating first US exports to 1995. The story attributes the 1996 milestone to Hikma's own timeline. Portugal: Hikma's 2015 annual report says a greenfield injectables plant was being built in 1990; the 2010 timeline says manufacturing began there in 1997; the story says only that building had begun. Darwazah's reasons and his quality wager come from the AUB profile, not from his own words; his memoir, Building a Global Success (2004), was not available online, and no interview in which he describes the 1978 decision could be found, so there are no direct founder quotations. Funding: no outside investor before the 2005 listing is named in any source, and AUB says small profits were reinvested, so the edition is marked bootstrapped; this is an inference. The barter details rest on the AUC case study as summarised by Wamda; the full case PDF was not available. Washington's passage concerns the reception of Black craftsmen's work in the American South; it is applied here only by analogy to trust earned through visible work.
